learningGoal.source: Explain how a shophouse joins a business and a home, connect a building's form with the street and the climate, and compare two trading cities without assuming they share one history.

read.sections.0.heading.source: The street is part of the architecture
read.sections.0.heading.back: The street is part of architecture

read.sections.0.text.note: five-foot way = ทางเดินห้าฟุต (literal). scale = ขอบเขต as in KEY_TERMS.
read.sections.0.text.source:
A building's front door connects private space to a wider street. Shops, paths, windows and entrances affect how people work, move and live near one another. A street is public space: space used by a wider community. So we can study architecture at the scale of one building and at the scale of a neighbourhood.

In George Town, Malaysia, shophouses are an important part of the historic town. A shophouse is a building that combines a business and a home. Traditionally, the business was below and the housing above. Shophouses are often narrow and long, and they stand in rows with shared walls. Airwells, open spaces inside the building, bring light and fresh air into deep rooms. Covered walkways, called five-foot ways, shelter people as they move along the fronts. A shop meets customers at the street, and an airwell deals with heat and light inside. These links connect a building's form with daily use.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A building's front door connects private space with the wider street. Shops, walkways, windows and entrances affect how people work, travel and live near each other. A street is public space, space a wider community shares. So we can study architecture at the scale of one building and at the scale of a whole district.

In George Town, Malaysia, shophouses are an important part of the old town. A shophouse is a building combining a shop and a home: originally the shop was downstairs and living quarters upstairs. Shophouses are often narrow and long, and stand in rows sharing walls. An airwell is an open space inside the building that brings light and fresh air to rooms deep inside. A covered walkway called the five-foot way shelters people walking past the front from sun and rain. The shop meets customers at the street, while the airwell deals with heat and light inside. These connections link the building's form with everyday use.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A front door joins a home to the street. Shops, paths, windows and doors shape how people work and live close together. A street is public space. That means it is a space for everyone. So we can study one building or a whole neighbourhood.

George Town is a city in Malaysia. It has many old shophouses. A shophouse is a shop and a home in one building. The shop was downstairs and the home was upstairs. Shophouses are narrow and long. They stand in rows and share walls. An airwell is an open space inside the house. It lets in light and fresh air. Covered paths run along the front. They give shelter to people walking past. They are called five-foot ways. Each part links the building to daily life.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
A front door connects a home with the street. Shops, walkways, windows and doors affect how people work and live near each other. A street is public space, meaning space for everyone. So we can study one building or a whole district.

George Town is a city in Malaysia. It has many old shophouses. A shophouse is a shop and a home in one building. The shop is downstairs and the home upstairs. Shophouses are narrow and long, stand in rows and share walls. An airwell is an open space inside the house that lets light and good air in. A roofed walkway runs along the front of the buildings, sheltering people walking past from sun and rain. This walkway is called the five-foot way. Each part connects the building with everyday life.

read.sections.1.heading.source: George Town: a port of many connections
read.sections.1.heading.back: George Town: a port city connected to many places

read.sections.1.text.note: multicultural = พหุวัฒนธรรม (simpler: หลายวัฒนธรรม); migrants = ผู้ย้ายถิ่น; Malay Archipelago = หมู่เกาะมลายู.
read.sections.1.text.source:
George Town grew as a British colonial port from the late eighteenth century. Its trade networks linked the Malay Archipelago, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European connections appear in the town's buildings and in practices that continue today. Places of worship, languages, festivals and neighbourhoods keep more specific histories within those broad labels. "Multicultural" describes these lives that met and mixed. It does not mean that each community arrived at the same time, shared one identity, or held equal political power under colonial rule.

Shophouses make this exchange easy to see. The local heritage organisation identifies early use by Indian and later by Chinese migrants, followed by changes involving European building experts. Owners redesigned façades, the fronts of buildings that face outwards, while keeping the mix of shop and home. The row in the photograph belongs to a history of change, not to one pure style from one homeland. A decorated front alone cannot tell us every builder's background or who lives there now.
read.sections.1.text.back:
George Town grew as a port city in a British colony from the late 18th century. Its trade networks joined the Malay world, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European connections appear in the city's buildings and in practices that continue today. Places of worship, languages, festivals and districts keep more specific histories under those broad group names. The word “multicultural” describes these lives meeting and mixing, but doesn't mean every community arrived at the same time, had the same identity, or had equal political power under colonial rule.

Shophouses make this exchange easy to see. A local heritage organisation says Indian and later Chinese migrants first used shophouses, then came changes in which European building specialists took part. Owners redesigned the façade, the front part facing outward, but still kept shop and home together. The row in the photograph is part of a history of change, not one pure style from one homeland. A decorated front alone can't tell every builder's background or who lives there now.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: "the late 1700s" = ช่วงปลายของปี 1700 ถึง 1799, following the KEY_TERMS pattern; a little heavy for the simpler text.
read.sections.1.simpler.source:
George Town grew as a British colonial port from the late 1700s. Ships linked it with the Malay world, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European links can be seen in its buildings. Places of worship, languages and festivals keep each group's own history. People call the town multicultural. But the groups did not all arrive at the same time. They did not share one identity. Under colonial rule, they did not have equal power.

Shophouses show this mixing. The local heritage group says Indian and then Chinese migrants used them early on. Later, European building experts changed them too. Owners changed the façades. A façade is the front of a building. But the shop and home stayed together. So the row in the photo shows change over time. A decorated front cannot tell us who built it. It cannot tell us who lives there now.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
George Town grew as a port city in a British colony from the late part of 1700 to 1799. Ships connected the city with the Malay world, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. We can see Malay, Chinese, Indian and European connections in the city's buildings. Places of worship, languages and festivals keep each group's history. People call the city multicultural, but the groups didn't arrive at the same time. They didn't have the same identity. Under colonial rule, they didn't have equal power.

Shophouses show this mixing. A local heritage group says Indian and later Chinese migrants first used shophouses. Later, European building specialists changed shophouses too. Owners changed the façade. The façade is the front part of a building. But the shop and home stayed together. So the row in the picture shows change over time. A decorated front can't tell who built it, and can't tell who lives there now.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Amsterdam: canals, trade and unequal wealth
read.sections.2.heading.back: Amsterdam: canals, trade and unequal wealth

read.sections.2.text.note: plantation goods = สินค้าจากไร่ขนาดใหญ่; enslaved people = ผู้คนที่ถูกบังคับเป็นทาส (sensitive: chosen over ทาส alone to keep "people who were enslaved").
read.sections.2.text.source:
For comparison, Amsterdam's canal district grew through a planned expansion of canals, streets, building plots and gabled houses, with shaped tops on their fronts. Its buildings also belong to a city network and to trade by sea. The photograph shows one part of that setting. It cannot prove each house's date, owner or first use.

Amsterdam's City Archives add a social history. Wealthy households lived on the wide canals, while craftspeople, shopkeepers and workers lived and worked in other streets. Some grand canal houses were paid for through trade in plantation goods produced by enslaved people. That link belongs in a story of trading wealth, even though the labour was far away and is missing from a handsome street view. It does not tell us how each pictured house was paid for.

The comparison connects buildings with work, movement, resources and unequal access to wealth. George Town's shophouses and Amsterdam's canal houses grew in different climates and political settings. Explaining these differences makes one shared question useful: how do trading streets organise private lives and wider connections? A street becomes clearer when we study its buildings and the people connected through them together.
read.sections.2.text.back:
For comparison, Amsterdam's canal district grew from a planned city expansion: canals, streets, building plots and gabled houses whose upper fronts have various shapes. Its buildings were also part of networks of cities and sea trade. The photograph shows part of that setting but can't prove the year built, owner or first use of each house.

The Amsterdam City Archives add social history. Rich families lived along the wide canals, while craftsmen, shopkeepers and workers lived and worked on other streets. Some large canal houses were built with money from trading plantation goods produced by enslaved people. That connection is part of the story of trade wealth, even though that labour was far away and doesn't appear in a pretty street picture; but it doesn't tell where the money for each house in the picture came from.

This comparison links buildings with work, travel, resources and unequal access to wealth. George Town's shophouses and Amsterdam's canal houses grew in different climates and political conditions. Explaining these differences makes one shared question useful: how do trading streets organise private life and wider connections? A street becomes clearer when we study the buildings and the people connected through them together.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Amsterdam is a city in the Netherlands. Its canal area was planned. People built canals, streets and tall houses with shaped tops. The houses were part of a trading city by the sea. The photo shows one part of it. It cannot tell us each house's date, owner or first use.

The city's records tell us more. Rich families lived on the wide canals. Workers and shopkeepers lived on other streets. Some big canal houses were paid for by trade in goods from plantations. Enslaved people were forced to grow those goods far away. That is part of the story. We just cannot see it in the street. But we do not know how each house in the photo was paid for.

The two cities had different weather and different rulers. In both, streets linked homes to trade. We understand a street better when we study its buildings and its people together.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Amsterdam is a city in the Netherlands. Its canal district was built to a plan. People built canals, streets and tall houses with various shapes at the top. These houses were part of a trading city by the sea. The photograph shows part of the city but can't tell when each house was built, who owned it or what it was first used for.

The city's records tell us more. Rich families lived along the wide canals. Workers and shopkeepers lived on other streets. Some large canal houses were built with money from trading plantation goods. Enslaved people were forced to grow those goods far away. That is part of the story; we just can't see it on the street. But we don't know where the money for each house in the picture came from.

These two cities have different weather and different rulers. Both have streets that connect homes with trade. We understand a street better when we study both the buildings and the people together.

write.prompt.source: Explain one way a George Town shophouse connects home life with the street. Use two features from the reading.
write.prompt.back: Explain one way a shophouse in George Town connects home life with the street. Use two features from the reading.

write.example.source: A shophouse has a shop on the ground floor. It opens onto the street, so customers walk in from the public space outside. It also has a covered five-foot way along the front. This path links it to the buildings next door and gives shelter to people walking past. Together, these connect the family's home upstairs with the busy street. The photo cannot show if each building is still used this way.
write.example.back: The shophouse has a shop downstairs. The shop opens onto the street, so customers walk in from the public space outside. The shophouse also has a covered five-foot way along the front. This walkway connects with the buildings next to it and shelters people walking past from sun and rain. Both of these connect the family's home upstairs with the busy street. The photograph can't show whether each building is still used this way.

visual.alt.source: A row of two-storey shophouses with orange tiled roofs. Upstairs, each has three arched windows with wooden shutters, set in pale green and blue plaster with moulded decoration. Downstairs are shop fronts and doors, one with a signboard in Malay and Chinese. A car and motorcycles are parked in front.
visual.alt.back: A row of two-storey shophouses with orange tiled roofs. Each upper floor has three arched windows with wooden shutters, on light green and blue plaster walls with moulded decoration. The ground floor has shopfronts and doors; one has signs in Malay and Chinese. Cars and motorbikes are parked in front.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: the mix of home and business; the shop facing the street; the covered walkway linking buildings; the airwell and the deep plan, where clearly linked. Don't assume every photographed building still has its first use.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: combining home and shop, shops facing the street, a covered walkway joining buildings, airwells and deep plans, if connected clearly. Don't assume every building in the photograph is still used in its original way.

educatorNotes.2.source: George Town World Heritage Incorporated's Shophouses page supports the mixed uses, the narrow, deep plan, airwells, covered walkways and changing styles; its own drawings and photographs are not used. UNESCO's Melaka and George Town page and George Town World Heritage Incorporated's page about the site support the trade links and the town's many practices; their language of harmony is not evidence that colonial power or wealth was shared equally.
educatorNotes.2.back: George Town World Heritage Incorporated's Shophouses page supports mixed use, narrow deep plans, airwells, covered walkways and changing styles; its drawings and photographs aren't used. UNESCO's Melaka and George Town page and George Town World Heritage Incorporated's page on the heritage area support the city's trade connections and varied practices. Their language of harmony isn't evidence that colonial-era power or wealth was shared equally.

educatorNotes.3.source: UNESCO's Amsterdam Canal Ring page supports the canals, the planned expansion and the gabled houses. The Amsterdam City Archives page supports the different districts and the link between some grand houses, plantation goods and enslaved labour. Neither identifies how the photographed houses were paid for or who first lived in them: don't call every pictured house a seventeenth-century merchant's home.
